title: Project executive, chief product owner, senior supplier and project assurance
blurb: Explain what the four governance-level roles do, and tell the CPO from the executive and assurance from support.
question: Three delivery teams are each designing their own screens and the branding no longer matches. Which role should make sure priorities are set consistently across all the teams?

teach.body: Four of the 11 PRINCE2 Agile roles work at governance level, above day-to-day management. The project executive is accountable for the project. The chief product owner (CPO) represents the users. The senior supplier represents those who design, build and deliver the products. Project assurance checks, independently of the project manager, that the project follows PRINCE2 Agile principles and agile practices.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 7.2, Table B.1

teach.h: Who does what at governance level
head: Role
Core job
Example responsibility
rows: Owns the project backlog; priorities across teams
Checks adherence to principles and practices
teach.caption: Paraphrased from Table 7.2 and Table B.1.

teach.h: Project executive: accountable and a role model
teach.body: The project executive is accountable for the project and its strategic alignment. They approve the project brief, the management approaches and the project management team structure, and they approve the tolerances for agile decision-making. In starting up, the executive leads the development of the project canvas from the mandate. They are also expected to model the agile adoption the project needs.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table B.1, Table 13.1

teach.h: Chief product owner: the voice of the users
teach.body: The CPO represents the user community and owns the project backlog. They keep it refined regularly with user input and aligned with each team's product backlog, and they make sure priorities are clearly defined across teams, for example consistent branding everywhere. It is the CPO, not the project manager, who makes sure user requirements are met.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 7.2, Table B.1, 5.2.1.3

teach.body: The senior supplier represents the supplier side: the people who design, develop and deliver the products, and the resources they bring. The PM consults the senior supplier, with the CPO and executive, when creating the project backlog. Project assurance monitors adherence to PRINCE2 Agile principles and agile practices, builds quality and governance checks into iterative delivery, and advises the board and PM on issues, risks, exception reports and impacts on the project canvas.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table B.1, Table 13.1

teach.body: Northmoor Libraries Trust is building a digital lending service with two delivery teams. Chief executive Helen Marsh, the project executive, approves the tolerances within which teams decide. Head of reader services Tomasz Wilk is the CPO: he owns the project backlog and settles a clash over search features between the teams. The software house's director Abena Clarke is the senior supplier. Quality lead Gareth Pryce provides assurance, checking that iterations include agreed quality reviews.

teach.text: The CPO prioritizes ACROSS teams and represents users; the product owner owns ONE team's backlog. The executive approves tolerances but does not prioritize the backlog. Assurance checks independently; it does not do the admin (that is project support).

items: Project executive: accountable; approves brief, approaches, team structure and agile tolerances.
CPO: represents users, owns the project backlog, sets priorities across teams.
CPO, not the PM, makes sure user requirements are met.
Senior supplier: represents those who design, build and deliver.
Project assurance: monitors principles and practices; quality and governance checks in iterations.
Assurance advises on issues, risks, exception reports and project canvas impacts.

summary: You can now explain the responsibilities of the project executive, CPO, senior supplier and project assurance. You can also tell the CPO from the product owner and assurance from support.

A.q: Which role owns the project backlog?
A.why: The CPO owns the project backlog and keeps it refined with user input (Table B.1).

whyNot.0: The product owner owns a team's product backlog, not the project backlog.
whyNot.1: The PM consults on backlogs and management approaches but does not own the project backlog.
whyNot.3: The executive is accountable for the project but does not own the backlog.

A.q: Which role approves the tolerances for agile decision-making?
A.why: Approving tolerances for agile decision-making is a project executive responsibility (Table B.1).

whyNot.1: The CPO sets priorities across teams; tolerances are approved by the executive.
whyNot.2: Assurance monitors and advises; it does not approve tolerances.
whyNot.3: The senior supplier represents the supplier side; it does not approve agile tolerances.

A.q: Which is a responsibility of project assurance in PRINCE2 Agile?
options: Updating the project and team dashboards
Owning and refining the project backlog
Approving the project management team structure
A.why: Project assurance monitors adherence to PRINCE2 Agile principles and agile practices (Table B.1).

whyNot.0: Updating and pulling information from dashboards is project support.
whyNot.2: Owning and refining the project backlog is the CPO's job.
whyNot.3: Approving the team structure is a project executive responsibility.

B.q: Four delivery teams are each choosing different colours and logos for their screens. Which role should make sure priorities are clearly defined across the teams?
B.why: The CPO makes sure priorities are clearly defined across teams (Table 7.2).

whyNot.0: Each PO looks after one team's backlog and does not prioritize across teams.
whyNot.1: The executive approves agile tolerances; consistent priorities across teams are the CPO's job.
whyNot.2: The PM is a servant leader linking governance and teams, not the one who prioritizes.

B.q: Which role represents the user community in a PRINCE2 Agile project?
B.why: The CPO represents the user community (Table 7.2).

whyNot.0: The senior supplier represents those who design, build and deliver the products.
whyNot.2: Project assurance monitors adherence and advises; it does not represent users.
whyNot.3: The team coach supports one or two delivery teams in self-managing.

B.q:
Which two statements about governance-level roles are correct?
1. The CPO keeps the project backlog aligned with the team product backlogs.
2. Project assurance compiles lists and administers workshops.
3. The project executive approves the management approaches.
4. The senior supplier owns the project backlog.
B.why: The CPO aligns the project backlog with delivery-level product backlogs (1), and the executive approves the management approaches (3) (Table B.1).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is wrong: compiling lists and workshop admin is project support.
whyNot.1: Both are wrong: admin is project support, and the CPO owns the project backlog.
whyNot.2: Statement 4 is wrong: the CPO owns the project backlog.

C.q: A project needs someone to make sure user requirements are met and someone to commit the supplier's people. Which roles are these?
C.why: The CPO makes sure user requirements are met (5.2.1.3), and the senior supplier represents the supplier side and its resources.

whyNot.1: The PM runs the project day to day, and the executive is accountable overall; neither commits supplier people.
whyNot.2: The PO works at team level, and assurance monitors adherence rather than committing resources.
whyNot.3: The executive approves tolerances, and the team coach supports self-management.

C.q: An exception report is being prepared. Which role advises the board on its impact on the project canvas, and which practice does the canvas belong to?
C.why: Project assurance advises the board and PM on exception reports and impacts against the project canvas (Table B.1), and the canvas is a business case practice artifact (6.3.2).

whyNot.0: Project support gives administrative help; it does not advise on canvas impacts.
whyNot.1: The agile coach removes organization-level blockers; the canvas is not a risk artifact.
whyNot.3: The CPO represents users; the canvas belongs to the business case practice, not organization.

C.q: In starting up a project, who leads the development of the project canvas, and from what?
options: Chief product owner; the project brief
C.why: The project executive leads the team in developing the project canvas based on the project mandate (Table 13.1).

whyNot.0: The CPO is consulted on the project backlog; the canvas comes from the mandate, led by the executive.
whyNot.1: The PM creates the project backlog with others; the release map is a plan, not the source of the canvas.
whyNot.3: The senior supplier is consulted, but does not lead the canvas or base it on a contract.

reteach.title: The owner, the customer, the builder and the inspector
reteach.question: Think of a house extension. Who pays and decides, who will live in it, who builds it and who checks it? Map them to the four roles.

blocks.body: The homeowner paying for it and accountable for the decision is the project executive. The family who will live in it, and who must agree the order of rooms, is the CPO. The building firm's director is the senior supplier. The independent inspector checking the work is done properly is project assurance.

blocks.text: The inspector checks; they do not fill in the paperwork. Checking is assurance; admin is project support.

explain.body: Accountable for the project. Approves the project brief, management approaches, team structure and the tolerances for agile decision-making.

test.q: Which role approves the project management team structure?
test.why: The project executive approves the project brief, management approaches and project management team structure (Table B.1).

whyNot.0: The PM prepares much of the content, but approval sits with the executive.
whyNot.1: Assurance monitors adherence and advises; it does not approve.
whyNot.2: The CPO represents users and owns the project backlog.

explain.body: Represents the users, owns the project backlog, keeps it aligned with team backlogs and sets priorities across teams.

test.q: What does the CPO keep the project backlog aligned with?
test.why: The CPO keeps the project backlog refined with user input and aligned with the delivery-level product backlogs (Table B.1).

whyNot.1: Project support provides admin; its schedule does not drive the backlog.
whyNot.2: The commercial management approach covers procurement and contracts, not backlog alignment.
whyNot.3: Training and coaching plans support agile maturity, not backlog alignment.

explain.body: Represents those who design, develop and deliver the products and the resources they bring. Consulted when the project backlog is created.

test.q: Whose interests does the senior supplier represent?
options: The users of the final product
Those who design, build and deliver
test.why: The senior supplier represents the supplier side: those who design, develop and deliver the products.

whyNot.0: Users are represented by the chief product owner.
whyNot.2: The business view and accountability sit with the project executive.
whyNot.3: Independent checking is project assurance, not the senior supplier.

explain.body: Monitors adherence to principles and agile practices, builds quality and governance checks into iterations, and advises on issues, risks and exceptions.

items: Monitor adherence to principles and practices
Feedback to balance agility and control

test.q: Which phrase BEST describes project assurance in PRINCE2 Agile?
options: Administrative support for iterations and workshops
Removing systemic blockers to agile adoption
Balancing agility with control through checks
Prioritizing user stories across delivery teams
test.why: Assurance integrates quality and governance checks into iterative delivery and gives feedback to balance agility with control (Table B.1).

whyNot.0: Administrative support tailored to iterations and workshops is project support.
whyNot.1: Removing systemic blockers is the agile coach's work.
whyNot.3: Prioritizing across teams is the CPO's responsibility.
